extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, novelists, and students of narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and executing a narrative method (dramatic/scene-based vs. pictorial/authorial narration) appropriate to a novel's subject, scope, and needs, with attention to point of view, consistency, and background-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a narrator only when the narrator adds value
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the presence of a seer and a recorder is made a value in itself, contributing definitely to the effect of the subject, he is better dispensed with and put out of the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the narrator's voice, commentary, or framed perspective materially contributes to the reader's experience. If not, avoid an intrusive narrator. Examples/anti-patterns: an omniscient spokesman who 'talks and talks' about an issue that might be revealinging itself without him; the narrator who exists merely for the convenience of the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign point of view to the reader via dramatic enactment when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: An undramatic subject can be treated dramatically, so that the different method is at hand; leave the characters to enact the story and assign the point of view to the reader himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the story's progress lies chiefly in visible behaviour or in incidents that can be shown, prefer scene-based dramatization that lets readers infer interior states. Use gestures, looks, and actions to enact inner life rather than explicit description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pictorial (panoramic) subjects from dramatic (action-driven) ones
rubrics_metrics.description: A large, loose, manifold subject, extensive in time and space, full of crowds and diversions, is a pictorial subject and can be nothing else; if a subject passes a certain reach it exceeds the capacity of the straight and dramatic method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match method to scope: wide-ranging chronicles, multi-generational sagas, or stories requiring broad survey need an authorial angle or chronicler to synthesize and summarize; compact, situation-based stories suit the dramatic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express interiority objectively through visible signs
rubrics_metrics.description: The story that is concerned with the impact of experience upon a mind can be enhanced to the pitch of drama because thought has its tell-tale gestures and its speaking looks, just as much as an actor on the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you wish to dramatize inner experience, identify externalized, repeatable behaviours (gestures, looks, small acts) that convey the mental process. Use these to 'enact' thought so the reader sees mental life without expository intrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistency of method within a work
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject asks for no more than to be reflected and pictured, the narrator standing in front of the story may be a value; but when a novelist chooses a method (e.g., pure drama) he should keep to it for homogeneity and truth to the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early whether the piece will be principally dramatic, pictorial, or mixed, and avoid casual switching that undermines unity. Pure dramas like The Awkward Age show the power of a homogeneous method; mixed methods must be justified by subject requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a direct view when it illuminates the subject best
rubrics_metrics.description: Where other things are equal a direct view of the matter in hand is the best. If the presence of a narrator is not an added value, it is better dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to showing rather than telling when a direct, dramatic presentation gives a clearer, stronger impression. Use narration only when it supplies synthesis, context, or an effect that scenes alone cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narration to supply background, generalization, and breadth that scenes cannot easily provide
rubrics_metrics.description: For placing and establishing a piece of action [the novelist's] seeing eye, which can sweep broadly and generalize the sense of what it sees, will meet this difficulty more naturally. Drama is narrow and can have no great depth of atmosphere without supplementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the effect of the action depends on its time, place, or a social atmosphere that must be clearly apprehended, employ authorial description or pictorial summary to establish setting and associations that scenes cannot fully render.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limitation of pure drama for conveying background and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The play-form—and with it fiction that is purely dramatic in its method—is hampered in its power to express the outlying associations of its scene. From the point of view of the reader the dramatic scene is vivid and compact; but it is narrow, it can have no great depth, and the colour of the atmosphere can hardly tell within the space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If background, social texture, or long-term conditions are integral to meaning, do not rely solely on dialogue and action; supplement with panoramic description or selective authorial commentary, or accept the extra difficulty of conveying such breadth purely scenically.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the subject is action-essential and compact, avoid the narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: The story that is concerned, even entirely concerned, with the impact of experience upon a mind... when the subject is action merely, and an action strictly limited in its scope, it requires no narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tight, situation-driven plots (e.g., a clear question that the characters' behaviour answers), present events scenically and let the action itself provide motive and meaning rather than explanatory narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of using omniscience for authorial convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an easy-going reliance on a narrator of some kind, a showman who is behind the scenes of the story and can tell us all about it. He seems to come forward in many a case without doing the story any particular service; sometimes he actually embarrasses it, when a matter of vivid drama is violently forced into the form of a narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting explanatory or judgmental asides simply to tidy plot holes or shortcut dramatic exposition. If omniscience is used, ensure it enriches the reader's experience rather than rescuing the author from the harder work of dramatizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the novelist's pictorial faculty to mass background force where it will propel drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the subject requires to be lodged securely in its surroundings, wherever the background is a main condition of the story, [Balzac] is in no hurry to precipitate the action; that can always wait, while he allows himself the leisure he needs for massing the force which is presently to drive the drama on its way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When action will derive its power from a richly established scene or society, invest narrative space in creating that setting so the subsequent drama carries full weight and immediacy (example: Balzac's preparation of the Maison Vauquer before Goriot's tale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance liberty and restraint: the novelist can control manner but pays dramatic costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist, using [dramatic] method, claims only one advantage over the playwright; it is the advantage of ensuring the very best acting imaginable... Otherwise the novelist completely ties his hands, submitting to all the restraints of the playwright in order to secure the compactness and the direct force of true drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the gain in control over manner and tone against the constraints imposed by strict scenicism. If control of delivery and nuance matters, accept some narration; if immediacy and compact action are paramount, accept the restrictions of drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize without losing necessary context—know when to allow background to be 'implied'
rubrics_metrics.description: Nanda’s little world would be descried behind the scene without any further picturing. He [James] may have been right... the behaviour of the people in the story is certainly packed with many meanings, and perhaps it is vivid enough to enact the general character of their lives and ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes behaviour and well-chosen details can imply a full background; be judicious about how much to state explicitly. If implied context suffices for reader comprehension and effect, spare exposition; otherwise supply more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that strict dramatic method is difficult and may be impractical for many authors
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat a subject with the rigour of Henry James is extremely difficult, and the practice of the thousand thousand is partly to be explained by this fact. Perhaps many of them would be more dramatically inclined if the way were easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic about technical demands: choosing pure drama as a method often requires exceptional skill in making actions and gestures do heavy narrative work. Don't choose that method for convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting incidental or background characters carry irrelevant past associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the characters in the remoter planes of the action... no more is expected than their value for the purpose of the action in the foreground. Whatever more they may bring will lie idle, will contribute nothing, and may even become an embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reusing or referencing characters (as Balzac does), ensure their pasts and associations are relevant to the current foreground action; avoid distracting the reader with extraneous histories that break unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value economy: use method that makes the most of the subject with least unnecessary apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: He [the narrator] represents the great principle of economy, and is a value in himself, and does contribute to the effect. But where there is no positive reason for him there is a reason, equally positive, for a different method, one that assigns the point of view to the reader himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the narrator or dramatization that accomplishes desired effects efficiently. If the narrator saves repeated exposition or clarifies complex relations, he serves economy; if he merely adds bulk, discard him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenic particularization intermittently to give objectivity even in subjective narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Pater... the scenes of the story reach the reader by refraction... when Marius takes a journey, visits a philosopher or enters a church, the event stands out of the past and makes an appeal to the eye, is presented as it takes place; and this is a movement in the direction of drama, even if it goes no further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in largely meditative or subjective narratives, punctuate ruminations with concrete episodes or images that anchor the story physically and give readers objective access to events and turning points.
